passage:
Looking back, last year I tried to be everywhere.
Charu, my manager, mentioned that senior roles need visibility. I heard it as "do everything leadership can see." So I joined the culture committee, volunteered for the CEO's offsite logistics, took the hackathon, and offered to help with the new client pitch. All on top of my actual job, the claims-processing redesign.
By October I was answering emails at 1 a.m. I missed the redesign pilot date. Then I sent the pitch numbers two days late, and Charu had to present with half a slide.
In my review she was kind but clear. "Jagdish, your list is long, but I can't point to one thing you owned from start to finish. It looks scattered."
I felt my face heat up. She was right.
This year, one project, the redesign, done properly.

qa.q: What was Jagdish's actual job last year?
qa.a: The claims-processing redesign.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel when Charu called the record scattered?
qa.a: Jagdish felt embarrassed, face heating up, and also recognised with some regret that she was right.

qa.q: What else could Jagdish have done after hearing that senior roles need visibility?
qa.a: Jagdish could have asked Charu what visibility meant in practice and which one project would show it, instead of guessing and saying yes to everything.

qa.q: How was Charu affected by Jagdish taking on too much?
qa.a: Charu had to present the client pitch with half a slide because the numbers came two days late, and then had to give a hard review.

grounding: It shows someone chasing every high-profile task, missing two deadlines and ending with a record that looks scattered rather than strong.
